title: Work stealing and thread pools
summary: How thread pools keep every core busy: per-worker deques, owners popping newest while thieves steal oldest, the Chase-Lev deque and its fences, Tokio and Go run queues, and parking workers without lost wakeups.
outcomes: Explain why one locked queue caps pool throughput and static sharding wastes cores on uneven work
Compute speedup bounds from work and span and explain why thieves steal the oldest task
Trace Chase-Lev push, take and steal, including the last-task CAS race and why take needs a full fence
Describe Tokio and Go run queues: 256-slot rings, steal half, LIFO slot, global queue checks
Explain how searching counts and StoreLoad barriers prevent thundering herds and lost wakeups

lessons.title: Why a pool needs more than one shared queue

blocks.md:
A **thread pool** is a fixed set of worker threads created once and reused for many small jobs called **tasks** (a task is just a function plus its data). From the threads course you know that creating a thread costs a system call and a stack, so paying that per task is wasteful. A pool pays it once.

The question for this course is how the workers find their next task. The answer decides whether 64 cores give you 64 times the throughput or barely more than one.

The obvious design is one shared queue protected by a mutex. Every submit locks it to push, every worker locks it to pop. From the mutex course you know what happens under contention: only one thread is inside at a time, the lock's cache line bounces between cores, and losers end up sleeping on a futex.

That makes the queue a serial section. If each queue operation holds the lock for $c$ microseconds, the whole pool can never hand out more than $1/c$ tasks per microsecond, no matter how many workers you add.

blocks.title: Throughput: one locked queue vs per-worker queues

scenes.caption: Simplified model with made-up but plausible costs: 1 us tasks and 0.2 us of serialized queue work. The shared queue caps at 1/c = 5 tasks per us once P passes (s+c)/c = 6 workers.
With 10 us tasks the cap is still 5 per us, but 32 workers only demand about 3.1 per us, so one queue is fine. Contention bites when tasks are short.
Halve both costs: the cap doubles to 1/c = 10 per us, but the knee stays at P = (0.5 + 0.1)/0.1 = 6, because the ratio s/c sets how many workers one queue can feed. Per-worker queues keep scaling.

blocks.md: Misconception: more workers always means more throughput. With one locked queue, past the knee extra workers only add waiters on the same lock and the same cache line. The model here is deliberately simple, but the cap of 1/c is real for any serial section.

The fix is to **shard**: give each worker its own queue so the common path touches no shared lock. But a static split has its own failure. Suppose 12 tasks arrive and are dealt round-robin to 4 workers. Tasks t0, t4 and t8 take 8, 7 and 6 ms; the other nine take 1 ms each, 30 ms of work in total.

blocks.prompt: Round-robin puts t0, t4 and t8 all on worker 0. With no way to move tasks, when does the last task finish, and what would a perfect split of 30 ms over 4 workers give?
blocks.reveal: Worker 0 runs 8 + 7 + 6 = **21 ms** while workers 1 to 3 finish their three 1 ms tasks at 3 ms and then sit idle for 18 ms. A perfect split would be 30 / 4 = 7.5 ms, and no schedule can beat 8 ms because t0 alone takes 8. Static sharding wastes most of the machine whenever task sizes are uneven, which is the normal case.

blocks.title: Static sharding vs work stealing on 12 uneven tasks

scenes.caption: Static round-robin: worker 0 owns the three big tasks and finishes at 21 ms. Workers 1 to 3 are idle from 3 ms on.
Work stealing: each worker pops its newest task first. At 3 ms workers 1 and 2 run dry and steal the oldest tasks (t0, t4) from worker 0. Everything ends at 11 ms.
Stealing is not optimal: the lower bound is 8 ms (t0 alone), and 11 ms reflects the thieves starting late. Simplified: thieves here pick the fullest queue; real pools pick victims at random.

blocks.md:
**Work stealing** combines both ideas. Each worker owns a **deque** (double-ended queue) of tasks. The owner pushes and pops at one end, the **bottom**. A worker whose deque is empty becomes a **thief**: it picks another worker (the **victim**) and takes a task from the other end, the **top**.

Under load every worker stays on its own deque, so there is almost no sharing. Only when a worker runs dry does it touch someone else's data. Blumofe and Leiserson proved this scheme efficient for Cilk-style programs (JACM 1999), Arora, Blumofe and Plaxton made the deque non-blocking (1998), and Chase and Lev made it growable (2005).
Work stealing moves the cost of load balancing onto idle workers. Busy workers pay almost nothing; the worker with nothing to do is the one that goes looking.

blocks.question: A pool runs 8 workers on 2 us tasks, and its single locked queue costs 0.5 us of serialized work per task. Using the lesson's model, about how many workers can the queue keep busy?
options: All 8, since 2 us tasks are much longer than 0.5 us
About 5, since (s + c)/c = 2.5/0.5 = 5
About 2, since only one thread can hold the lock
About 4, since half the time is spent in the queue
blocks.explain: The queue hands out at most 1/c = 2 tasks per us, and each worker consumes 1/(s+c) = 0.4 tasks per us, so the queue saturates at 2/0.4 = 5 workers. The other 3 mostly wait on the lock.

blocks.question: Which workload gains the most from work stealing over static per-worker queues?
options: Millions of identical 1 ms tasks dealt evenly to workers
A single long task that cannot be split
Tasks that each hold a global lock for their whole run
A recursive divide-and-conquer job whose subproblems vary wildly in size
blocks.explain: Stealing fixes imbalance. Evenly dealt identical tasks have none, one unsplittable task cannot be shared, and a global lock serializes everything anyway. Uneven recursive work is exactly where idle workers find something to steal.

lessons.title: Owner pops newest, thief steals oldest: why the ends matter

blocks.md: Most work-stealing pools run **fork-join** code: a task splits its problem, runs the pieces in parallel, then waits for them. Rayon's `join(a, b)` is the canonical API. Its documentation describes what happens inside a worker: the worker starts running closure `a` itself and meanwhile **advertises** `b` on its deque so another thread may steal it. When `a` finishes, the worker runs `b` itself unless it was stolen, in which case it looks for other work while waiting for the thief.

blocks.caption: A toy fork-join program (real code would stop splitting below a size threshold). Every call except the leaves pushes one task.

blocks.md: Count the work in each pending task as the number of `fib` calls it will make: 1 for `fib(0)` and `fib(1)`, 3 for `fib(2)`, 5 for `fib(3)`, 9 for `fib(4)`, 15 for `fib(5)`. Watch worker 0's deque while it computes `fib(5)` alone, then a thief arrives.

scenes.caption: Worker 0 starts fib(5). The deque is empty: top equals bottom.
join(fib(4), fib(3)): push f(3) at the bottom, run fib(4) right away. f(3) is worth 5 calls.
Inside fib(4): push f(2) (3 calls), run fib(3).
Two more levels push f(1) and f(0). Worker 0 is now running the leaf fib(1). Older entries sit near the top and are bigger: 5, 3, 1, 1 calls.
A thief steals from the top and gets f(3): 5 of the 15 calls in one steal. top moves up by one; the owner never touched that end.
Worker 0 finishes its leaf and pops f(0) from the bottom: the newest, smallest task, whose data it touched a moment ago.

blocks.prompt: Why should thieves take the oldest task rather than the newest?
blocks.reveal: In divide-and-conquer code the oldest pending task was pushed highest in the recursion, so it is the **biggest** piece left (f(3) above, 5 calls versus 1 for f(0)). One steal moves a large chunk of work, so thieves need few steals. Taking from the opposite end also means owner and thief only compete when a single task is left, which is what makes the Chase-Lev deque cheap (next lesson).

blocks.md: The owner's choice matters too. Popping the newest task (LIFO) makes each worker execute its subtree depth-first, in the same order as the serial program. That keeps recently touched data in cache and bounds memory: Blumofe and Leiserson show the space used on $P$ processors is at most $S_1 P$, where $S_1$ is the stack space of the serial run. A FIFO owner would instead expand the tree breadth-first and could hold exponentially many pending tasks.

To say how fast this is, two numbers describe any fork-join computation. The **work** $T_1$ is the total time of all instructions (the run time on one processor). The **span** $T_\infty$ is the length of the longest chain of dependencies (the run time with infinitely many processors). Their ratio $T_1/T_\infty$ is the **parallelism**: the most speedup the program could ever get.

blocks.caption: Left: no schedule can beat the work divided by P or the span. Right: Blumofe and Leiserson's bound for randomized work stealing, which is within a constant factor of optimal.

blocks.md:
The same paper bounds the expected number of steal attempts by $O(P\,T_\infty)$. Steals are tied to the span, not the work: a program with a lot of work and a short span needs few steals, so the cost of stealing disappears into the $T_1/P$ term.

Worked example: sum $2^{20}$ numbers by splitting in half recursively down to leaves of 1024 numbers, at one time unit per addition. Work $T_1 \approx 2^{20} = 1{,}048{,}576$. The span is one leaf plus 10 levels down and 10 back up: $T_\infty = 1024 + 20 = 1044$, so the parallelism is about 1004.

blocks.title: Speedup bound T1 / (T1/P + Tinf) for the 2^20 sum

scenes.caption: Taking the hidden constant as 1 for illustration: at P = 64 the bound gives 60.2x, nearly linear, because P is far below the parallelism of about 1004.
At P = 1024 (about the parallelism) the span term equals the work term and speedup is only 507x. At 4096 it is 806.6x. Beyond the parallelism, more processors barely help.
Leaves of 10240 numbers make the span about 10x longer and parallelism about 100: speedup now flattens near 100. Coarse tasks cut overhead but also cut parallelism.

blocks.md: The bound assumes stealing is cheap relative to tasks. If tasks are a few nanoseconds each, the deque operations themselves dominate. Real libraries stop splitting below a grain size; picking it is a tradeoff between overhead (too small) and parallelism (too large).

blocks.question: A worker's deque holds, from top to bottom, tasks of 40, 20, 10 and 5 units pushed by one recursive split. A thief steals once and the owner pops once. Which tasks do they get?
options: Thief 5, owner 40
Thief 40, owner 5
Thief 40, owner 20
Both race for 5
blocks.explain: Thieves take from the top, where the oldest and here largest task (40) sits. The owner pops the bottom, the newest (5). They only contend when exactly one task is left.

blocks.question: A program has work 10^9 units and span 10^6 units. Roughly how many processors can it use well?
options: About 1,000, its parallelism T1/Tinf
About 10^6, the span
Any number, since work stealing scales linearly
About 30, since the span is log2 of the work
blocks.explain: Speedup is limited by T1/Tinf = 1000. Below about 1000 processors the T1/P term dominates and speedup is near linear; above it the span term dominates.

lessons.title: The Chase-Lev deque: two counters and one CAS

blocks.md: The **Chase-Lev deque** (SPAA 2005) is the data structure under most work stealers. It has three fields: a circular array whose size is a power of two, and two integer counters. **bottom** is the next free slot, written only by the owner. **top** is the oldest task, and it only ever increases. The deque holds the tasks at positions top up to bottom minus 1, stored at array index position mod size; it is empty when bottom is at most top.

Because top never decreases, a thief's compare-and-swap (CAS) from $t$ to $t+1$ can never be fooled by top leaving and returning to the same value. From the lock-free course you know this as the **ABA problem**; the earlier ABP deque needed an extra tag field to avoid it, Chase-Lev needs none. The paper notes the only limit on deque size is counter overflow, which a 64-bit counter makes irrelevant in practice.

When a push finds the array full, the owner allocates one twice as large and copies the live positions. Since slots are position mod size, top and bottom stay unchanged; tasks just land at new indices. In the paper's version a push grows the array when it holds size minus 1 tasks, always leaving one cell unused.

blocks.title: Growing the circular array from 4 to 8 slots

scenes.caption: top = 5, bottom = 8: three tasks at positions 5, 6, 7, stored at 5 mod 4 = 1, 2 and 3. Three tasks in a size-4 array is full by the paper's rule.
Pushing D triggers grow: copy positions 5, 6, 7 into a size-8 array, where 5 mod 8 = 5, 6 and 7. top and bottom are untouched.
D goes to position 8, index 8 mod 8 = 0, and bottom becomes 9. The old array cannot be freed yet: a thief may still be reading from it.

blocks.md: Here are push and steal in portable C11, as published by Lê, Pop, Cohen and Zappa Nardelli (PPoPP 2013). They formally proved their hand-tuned ARMv7 version correct on a weak memory model and explain how that proof carries over to this C11 version. Push needs no atomic read-modify-write at all. Steal needs one CAS on top.

blocks.caption: From Lê et al., Figure 1 (atomic_ and memory_order_ prefixes elided as in the paper; indices shown as signed long here so that bottom minus 1 cannot wrap).

blocks.md: **take** is the owner's pop from the bottom. Its trick is to reserve the slot first by lowering bottom, then read top. If at least one other task remains, no thief can reach slot b, so the owner returns it without any CAS. Only when it is taking the last task does it race the thieves with the same CAS on top that they use. Step through two takes from a deque with top = 4 and bottom = 6.

blocks.title: take: the cheap path and the last-task race

scenes.caption: First take. Two tasks at positions 4 and 5. The owner lowers bottom to 5, claiming position 5 before looking at top.
The full fence orders the store to bottom before the load of top. t = 4.
t is less than b, so another task remains and no thief can be reaching for position 5. Return it with no CAS: the common case costs one fence.
Second take, one task left at position 4. Now t == b: a thief that read top = 4 may want the same task.

scenes.output: cas(top, 4, 5) failed: a thief got there first
scenes.caption: Both sides CAS top from 4 to 5 and exactly one wins. Here the thief won, so the owner returns EMPTY.
The owner sets bottom = b + 1 = 5, the canonical empty state. Win or lose, top is 5 now, so the deque is consistent.

blocks.md: Owner and thieves only ever race for the last task. Every other take is a store, a fence and a load with no CAS, and a push needs no read-modify-write at all.

blocks.prompt: The full fence in take sits between storing bottom and loading top. On x86 a store can wait in the core's store buffer while a later load already reads memory. Remove the fence. Can a task be run twice?
blocks.reveal: Yes. Start with tasks A and B at positions 3 and 4 (top = 3, bottom = 5). The owner's store bottom = 4 waits in its store buffer while it loads top = 3, sees two tasks and takes B with no CAS. Meanwhile a thief steals A (top becomes 4), steals again, still reads the old bottom = 5, and its CAS from 4 to 5 succeeds: **B runs twice**. This is the store-buffering pattern; Lê et al. note that x86 needs exactly one mfence, in take.

blocks.title: Without the fence in take, one task is taken twice

scenes.caption: Start: top = 3, bottom = 5, tasks A (3) and B (4). The owner's store of bottom = 4 is buffered, not yet visible to other cores.
With no fence the owner's load runs ahead of its own store. It sees two tasks, so it takes B without a CAS.
The thief reads top = 3 and bottom = 5, and steals A. So far fine.
The thief steals again. bottom still reads 5, so position 4 looks available and its CAS succeeds. Owner and thief both hold B.
The buffered store drains. With the seq_cst fence, the store would be visible before the owner read top, and the second steal would have seen an empty deque.

blocks.md:
Two more practical problems. First, **reclaiming old arrays**: after a grow, a slow thief may still hold a pointer to the old array, so it cannot be freed immediately. Chase and Lev's basic version relies on a garbage collector. Rust's crossbeam-deque grows (minimum capacity 64) and also shrinks, and frees old buffers through epoch-based reclamation. Tokio's blog explains that this reclamation adds atomic work to every operation, which is one reason Tokio dropped growth entirely (next lesson).

Second, **steal can fail spuriously**: losing the CAS returns ABORT (crossbeam calls it `Steal::Retry`), and the thief should retry or move on, not conclude the deque is empty.

blocks.question: A thief's steal returns ABORT. What is the correct conclusion?
options: Another thread won the CAS on top; the deque may still hold tasks, so retry or try elsewhere
The victim's deque is empty, so stop trying it
The deque is corrupted and must be reset
The owner is resizing, so the thief must wait on a lock
blocks.explain: ABORT (Retry in crossbeam) only means this thief lost a race on top, against another thief or the owner taking the last task. Treating it as empty can make a worker park while work remains.

blocks.question: Why can the owner's take skip the CAS when t < b after lowering bottom?
options: Because thieves only read, they never write top
Because the owner holds a lock on the bottom half
Because a thief can only claim position top, by CAS, and with t < b position b is not top, so no thief can be reaching for slot b
Because x86 makes all loads atomic
blocks.explain: Thieves only take position top and must win a CAS to move it. With t < b at least two positions remain, so a thief racing now gets position t, never b. The fence guarantees the owner's reservation of b and a thief's view of bottom are ordered.

lessons.title: Production run queues: fixed rings, steal half, a LIFO slot

blocks.md: Tokio, Rust's async runtime, first used crossbeam's growable deque. When its scheduler was rewritten in 2019, the author found growth was not worth its cost and adapted the Go runtime's fixed-size queue instead. The current Tokio documentation describes the multi-thread runtime like this: one global queue, plus one local queue per worker that holds **at most 256 tasks**.

blocks.title: Where a Tokio worker looks for its next task

nodes.label:
task woken
by a running task

scenes.caption: When a task wakes another (say by sending on a channel), the woken task goes to the LIFO slot and runs next, while the message is still in cache. A task already in the slot is pushed to the local queue.
If the 256-slot local queue is full, half of it plus the new task (129 tasks) moves to the global queue under one mutex acquisition.

The worker checks the global queue when its local queue is empty, and also periodically: every global_queue_interval tasks. By default this is self-tuned from the mean poll time; the source targets about 200 us between checks, clamped to 2 to 127 tasks.
With both queues empty, the worker steals half the tasks of another worker's local queue, starting from a random victim and trying each in turn.

blocks.md: Tokio's ring is single-producer, multi-consumer: the owner pushes at the tail, and both the owner's pop and thieves' steals take from the head with a CAS. Pushing is just an acquire load of head and a release store of tail. On a full queue the owner moves half the tasks to the global queue rather than growing. The Tokio source currently keeps the older half locally and sends the newer half, so a task just pulled from the global queue is not immediately bounced back.

A steal takes $n - \lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ of the victim's $n$ tasks (Go's `runqgrab` uses the same expression), so half rounded up. The thief runs one of them immediately and makes the rest available in its own queue, which other idle workers can then steal from. A thief whose own queue is already more than half full does not steal.

blocks.title: Steal half: a victim with 7 tasks (8-slot ring for illustration)

scenes.caption: Victim holds 7 tasks at positions 0 to 6. Real Tokio and Go rings have 256 slots; 8 keeps the picture readable.
One CAS moves the victim's head from 0 to 4, claiming n - floor(n/2) = 7 - 3 = 4 tasks. Tokio packs two head values into one word so other thieves back off while the copy is in progress.
The four tasks are copied into the thief's ring. The thief runs the last one (t3) itself and publishes t0 to t2 by storing its tail, so 3 remain for other thieves.

blocks.md: Tokio's local queue is FIFO, not LIFO: the owner pops from the same end thieves steal from. For servers made of many independent tasks, fairness (no task waits forever behind newer ones) matters more than depth-first order. Locality comes from the LIFO slot instead, which Tokio uses at most 3 times in a row to prevent two tasks from starving the queue by waking each other.

Go's scheduler, the source of this design, has the same shape. Each P (a scheduling context, one per GOMAXPROCS) has a 256-entry `runq` ring plus a `runnext` slot that plays the role of the LIFO slot. Every 61st scheduling tick a P checks the global run queue first, so goroutines there are not starved. Idle Ms (OS threads) try stealing half of another P's queue, making up to 4 passes over all Ps in a random order.

Libraries without an async-server focus expose the choice. crossbeam-deque offers `Worker::new_lifo()` and `Worker::new_fifo()` plus a global FIFO `Injector`. Java's ForkJoinPool is stack-based (LIFO) by default, and its `asyncMode` flag switches to local FIFO for event-style tasks that are never joined.

blocks.question: A Tokio worker's local queue is full (256 tasks) when it schedules one more. What happens?
options: The ring doubles to 512 slots
The new task waits until a slot frees up
128 queued tasks plus the new one, 129 in total, move to the global queue
Only the new task goes to the global queue, always
blocks.explain: Tokio never grows the ring. push_overflow claims the whole queue with one CAS, keeps the older 128 tasks locally and links the newer 128, plus the new task, into the mutex-protected global queue in one batch. (If a steal is already in progress the new task alone goes to the global queue, since the steal will free space.)

blocks.question: Why does Tokio steal half of a victim's queue rather than one task?
options: One steal rebalances a lot of work, so fewer steals and fewer cross-core cache misses are needed, and the thief can feed other thieves
Stealing one task at a time is not possible with a ring buffer
Half is required for the CAS to succeed
It guarantees both queues end with exactly equal length
blocks.explain: Each steal touches another core's cache lines, so batching amortizes that cost. The tasks land in the thief's own stealable queue, which lets work spread quickly: the next idle worker can steal from the thief.

blocks.question: A task keeps waking a partner task, which wakes it back, forever. Without a cap, what goes wrong with the LIFO slot?
options: Nothing, both tasks get CPU time
The two tasks could take turns in the LIFO slot and starve everything in the local queue; Tokio disables the slot after 3 uses in a row
The tasks are stolen by other workers
The global queue overflows
blocks.explain: The LIFO slot always runs before the local queue. Two tasks ping-ponging through it would monopolize the worker, so Tokio disables it after 3 consecutive uses until a task from elsewhere runs.

lessons.title: Parking idle workers without lost wakeups or thundering herds

blocks.md:
A worker that finds no task anywhere should stop burning CPU and **park**: sleep in the kernel until someone wakes it. From the futex course you know the primitive. Go's `mPark` calls `notesleep`, which on Linux is a loop around `futexsleep`, and waking calls `futexwakeup` on the same word. Tokio parks a worker on its I/O driver or, if another worker holds the driver, on a condition variable.

Parking is cheap; deciding **when to wake** whom is the hard part. Go's runtime comment states the dilemma: scheduler state is spread across per-worker queues, so no fast path can see a global picture, and ideal decisions would require knowing the future.

The naive rule is to wake a sleeper on every new task. Tokio's original scheduler did that, and also had each woken worker that found a task wake yet another. The 2019 rewrite describes the result: very quickly every worker was awake and searching, contending on the same queues, and most found nothing and went back to sleep. That is a **thundering herd**.

Both Go and Tokio now use the same rule, built on a count of **searching** (Go: spinning) workers, ones that are awake, out of local work and looking to steal:

1. When new work is submitted, wake one parked worker **only if no worker is searching** and some worker is idle.
2. A woken worker starts in the searching state.
3. When a searching worker finds work, it leaves the searching state and, if it was the last searcher, **wakes one more**.
4. Cap the searchers: Tokio refuses to start searching when twice the number of searchers is at least the number of workers; Go allows a new spinning thread while twice the spinners is below the number of busy Ps.

blocks.title: Wake one, steal half: 64 tasks spreading over 8 workers

scenes.caption: A batch of 64 tasks becomes ready on worker 0 (say after one epoll call). The first one triggers one notification: worker 1 wakes and enters the searching state. The rest notify nobody.
Worker 1 steals 64 - 32 = 32 tasks, leaves the searching state and notifies one more worker.
Worker 2 steals half of worker 0's 32: 16 tasks. It, too, stops searching and wakes the next.
Worker 3 steals 16 of worker 1's 32. Note the thief can steal from a previous thief.
Worker 4 takes 8 of worker 0's 16. Each wake brings exactly one more worker online.
Worker 5 takes 8 of worker 1's 16.
Worker 6 takes 8 of worker 2's 16.
After 7 wakes and 7 steals all 8 workers have 8 tasks. Simplified: tasks do not finish during the ramp, and thieves here pick the fullest victim; real ones start at a random victim.

blocks.md: The ramp is self-throttling: at most one notification is in flight at a time, so 7 wakes bring up 7 workers with no worker woken for nothing. The Tokio post calls this a smooth ramp up with rapid load balancing.

blocks.prompt: A searching worker gives up: it decrements the searcher count, checks the queues once more, finds them empty and parks. At the same moment another worker pushes a task, reads the searcher count and, seeing a searcher, wakes nobody. Can the task be stranded?
blocks.reveal: Yes, unless both sides use a full (StoreLoad) barrier. Each side writes one variable and then reads the other's. Without a barrier each read can return the value from before the other's write: the giver-up sees an empty queue, the submitter sees a searcher, and the task sits in a queue while every other worker sleeps. Go's runtime documents exactly this pattern: submit, then barrier, then check spinners; decrement spinners, then barrier, then recheck all queues.

blocks.title: The lost wakeup between a submitter and a giving-up searcher

scenes.caption: The searcher found nothing and decides to stop. Its decrement of the spinner count sits in its store buffer.
Meanwhile a busy worker pushes a new task into its queue. That store is also still buffered.
Each reads the other's variable before the other's store is visible: the submitter sees a searcher and wakes nobody; the searcher sees no work.
The searcher parks. If every other worker is asleep, the task waits until something unrelated wakes a worker.
Fix: a StoreLoad barrier between each side's write and read. Then at least one side sees the other's write: either the submitter sees zero spinners and wakes someone, or the searcher sees the task.

blocks.md: The searching count throttles wakeups, and the barrier on both sides of it prevents lost ones. Remove the throttle and you get a thundering herd; remove the barrier and you get stranded tasks with idle cores.

Common ways a work-stealing pool still goes wrong:

- **Blocking a worker.** A task that blocks on I/O or runs a long computation without yielding holds a worker hostage. Tokio's docs say this may prevent the executor from driving other futures and point to `spawn_blocking`, which runs the closure on a separate pool of blocking threads.
- **Tasks too small.** Every push, pop and steal has a cost; split work down to a grain size, not to single elements.
- **NUMA.** On NUMA (non-uniform memory access) machines, memory attached to another socket is slower to reach. Tokio's runtime docs state it is not NUMA aware and suggest starting multiple runtimes instead of one on such systems.
- **Sharing the counters.** top and bottom are hammered by different cores; keeping unrelated hot fields off the same cache line avoids false sharing.

blocks.question: A Tokio runtime has 8 workers and 4 of them are currently searching. A fifth idle worker tries to start searching. What happens?
options: It starts searching; there is no limit
It wakes all other parked workers first
It is refused, because 2 x 4 >= 8, so it goes back to parking
It steals from the global queue only
blocks.explain: transition_worker_to_searching returns false when 2 x num_searching >= num_workers, so at most about half the workers search at once. Tokio calls the limit sloppy on purpose: it is a throttle, not an exact bound.

blocks.question: A pool notifies a parked worker on every single push. A burst of 1,000 tasks arrives on one worker with 15 workers parked. What is the main problem?
options: Tasks are executed twice
All 15 workers can be woken at once and pile onto the same victim queue, and many go back to sleep empty-handed
Tasks are lost because the futex only wakes one thread
Nothing; more wakeups always help
blocks.explain: That is the thundering herd the Tokio 0.1 scheduler suffered. Waking only when nobody is searching, and letting each successful searcher wake the next, brings workers online one at a time as they find work.

blocks.question: Which change to the giving-up path reintroduces lost wakeups?
options: Removing the barrier between decrementing the searcher count and rechecking the queues
Starting the search at a random victim
Stealing half instead of one task
Capping searchers at half the workers
blocks.explain: The barrier makes the searcher's decrement visible before it rereads the queues, so a concurrent submitter either sees zero searchers (and wakes someone) or its task is seen by the recheck. The other choices affect efficiency, not correctness.

sources.label: Chase and Lev, Dynamic Circular Work-Stealing Deque (SPAA 2005)
